title: Announcing SAP Pay, Powered by Tereina
author: Yogananda
text:
SAP Pay was Introduced with the core vision during SAP Connect event on October 6, 2026 
 What is SAP Pay? 
 SAP Pay is the out-of-the-box B2B payments solution embedded in SAP Cloud ERP and provided by Tereina, an SAP entity dedicated to providing payment services, with OFAC and KYC/AML screening applied to every transaction. This gives SAP Cloud ERP customers a built-in way to automate payment execution across traditional and digital currency rails, with no separate implementation project, bank testing, or manual file uploads. Because SAP Pay runs natively inside the ERP environment, finance teams can initiate and manage payments without leaving their existing SAP workflow. 
 Access every payment rail—traditional and digital—through a single connection, with payment automation, reconciliation, and a unified know-your-customer process that: 
 Supports ACH, EFT, wire, check, and stablecoin payments like USD Coin (USDC). 
 Auto-reconciles every payment to its originating purchase order (PO) or invoice. 
 Covers 89 global corridors—no per-country bank setup required. 
 Autonomously initiates and executes payments using AI agents. 
 SAP Pay powered by Tereina 
 Reduce payment costs and drive payment automation with embedded, agentic B2B payments across traditional and digital currency rails. 

 Key features 

 Multi-rail payment support—your payment, your option SAP Pay supports fiat and digital currencies and many payment types. This includes real-time payments, alongside USDC stablecoin payments with native integration to Circle, and an intelligent routing to the optimal rail for each transaction across 40+ currencies—all from a single platform. 

 Natively embedded in SAP S/4HANA SAP Pay ships as an out-of-the-box capability inside SAP Cloud ERP, with secure bank communication handled via SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity. There’s no implementation project, no new vendor contract, and no custom code—customers activate it inside existing SAP workflow and it runs. 

 Agentic payment execution SAP Pay embeds payment execution into SAP now, the foundational step toward agentic payments. The AI agents that already support your finance team through Joule will soon trigger and execute payments, too, closing decision to execution in one flow. 
 References 
 SAP Pay 
 SAP Help Documentation 
 Security Guide & Setup Process 
 SAP Store - SAP Pay 

 Watch Demo - SAP Pay Stablecoin Payments 
 End-to-end demo of a stablecoin payment in SAP Cloud ERP The demo covers the payment of an open supplier invoice with SAP Pay as house bank: creation in the payment run, status tracking in the Payment Monitor, the transaction in the Tereina portal in USDC and USD, the on-chain transfer in the Circle wallet, the USDC wallet in SAP Short-Term Cash Positioning, and the end-of-day CAMT053 bank statement for posting. Payments are initiated, approved and reconciled in the standard SAP workflow, treasury sees the balance in its normal cash view, and settlement takes minutes instead of days. 
 FAQ 

 Is SAP Pay replacing SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity? 
 No, SAP Pay is using SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity for secure bank communication. SAP Pay provides customers another option to facilitate payments in addition to connecting to banks and payment service providers directly via SAP Multi-Bank Connectivity.

title: V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 3) : From Measured Quantities to Billing and Invoicing
author: Beaucamp99
text:
In the previous chapters , we went through the setup of the V2G-device configurations and the installation of those devices, ultimately allowing us to enter MR results in both kWh for charging and discharging and MIN for the availability bonus. 
 This chapter will be dedicated to the billing and invoicing aspect of the V2G-installations. As established in the previous chapter , three register-permissible rates were created with the sole purpose of registering the consumptions: 
 CO_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of charging quantity in kWh 
 COMP_V2G_E – Registering and transferring of discharging quantity in kWh 
 TIME_V2G_E – Registering of connection time in MIN and conversion to HRS 
 Billing schema E_V2G_SCH 

 Once the register-permissible rates have registered and transferred the quantities, a facts-permissible rate is required to calculate the amounts based on the measured quantities. 
 In the context of this V2G set-up, a new rate “E_V2G_BILL” was created. All rate steps calculating an amount simply use the QUANTI01 variant which allows for a quantity to be multiplied by a quantity-based price to calculate an amount. 
 IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL – rate steps 

 The following IS-U prices were configured in our SAP S/4HANA system and stored in the operands with type QPRICE at rate facts level: 
 E_V2G_C+ – Price for charging at 0,3297 EUR/kWh 

 E_V2G_C- – Price for discharging at -0,40 EUR/kWh 

 E_V2G_TCON – Price for availability bonus at -0,24/HR 

 Unlike the quantity-based prices used to calculate an amount based on the consumptions registered in kWh, price “E_V2G_TCON” must be configured with a UoM in HRS: 
 IS-U quantity-based price E_V2GTCON with UoM “hrs” 

 As established in the previous chapter ( V2G integration in IS-U Billing (Part 2): From Meter Reading Results to Billable Quantities ), the quantities originally registered in MIN will already have been converted by rate “TIME_V2G_E”. This allows us to directly apply a price per hour for the availability bonus. 
 Finally, to store the quantity-based price with a UoM of HRS, the QPRICE operand in which the price will be stored must have a matching UoM: 
 QPRICE Operand E_V2G_TPR 

 Overview of the rate facts in E_V2G_BILL: 
 IS-U Rate E_V2G_BILL – Rate facts within fact group V2G 

 After configuring the facts-permissible rate that calculates the amounts, a facts-permissible rate type will be required to create the rate determination. For these examples, rate type “E_V2G_EBIL” was created and stored in a RATETYPE operand in the installation facts of both installations for each respective scenario. 
 Rate determination for IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL 

 Installation 4100000512: 
 Installation 4100000512 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts 

 Installation 4100000513: 
 Installation 4100000513 – Operand E_V2G_RTYP maintained in Installation facts 

 The IS-U billing and invoicing runs can now be executed for both installations, regardless of the respective device configuration. When analysing the billing documents, we can now filter for the posting-relevant lines. These lines show the amounts calculated by multiplying the quantities registered in kWh by the corresponding quantity-based prices and, more importantly, the amount calculated based on the number of hours the vehicle has been connected to the grid for the availability bonus. 
 Scenario 1 – Billing document 100000005504 

 Scenario 2 – Billing document 100000005503 

 While we are still looking at the billing process, I would also like to highlight another interesting aspect of the availability bonus, namely the fact that the reimbursed connection time could be limited. As a possible commercial rule, the reimbursed connection time could be limited to 250 hours per month. With the hourly price used in this example, the availability bonus would therefore be capped at EUR 60 per month. This is also something I integrated in the E_V2G_BILL rate by adding the IF01 variant which allows us to compare the values of two quantity operands: 

 In this example, we compare the hourly quantity stored in operand E_V2G_CHR to the quantity stored in operand E_V2G_T250 . The latter is fixed at 250 hours in the rate category facts: 
 Rate category facts of E_V2G_RC : fixed quantity of 250 hours 

 If the number of hours registered for the availability bonus exceeds the limit of 250 hours, the amount is calculated based on the fixed quantity of 250 hours stored in E_V2G_T250 (rate step 5). Otherwise, the amount is calculated based on the originally measured number of hours stored in E_V2G_CHR (rate step 7). To illustrate this, if the meter reading result were 18.000 MIN, it would be converted to 300 HRS. In that case, the availability bonus would therefore be calculated based on 250 hours, while the remaining 50 hours would not be included in the calculation. 
 The example below illustrates what this could look like on a billing document: 
 Billing document 100000005502 – measured quantity of 18.000 MIN exceeding the 250-hour limit. 

 Before we move on to the results of the invoicing run for both scenarios, I would like to point out that for these examples I do not intend to apply any taxes for the availability bonus. On top of that, I also wanted to ensure that the lines for the availability bonus would be displayed on a separate line on the print document. 
 For that reason, I created dedicated FI-CA sub-transactions for the availability bonus: 
 Table TE305 – Sub-transactions for availability bonus: 0250 (Debit) – 0251 (Credit) 

 Using dedicated sub-transactions allows the availability bonus to be distinguished from the energy-related charges within the FI-CA and invoicing processes. And of course, these sub-transactions are configured on the lines that calculate the amount for the availability bonus in the E_V2G_BILL rate: 
 IS-U rate E_V2G_BILL - sub-transactions for availability bonus configured in the rate steps 

 In addition, a separate tax determination, “V0”, linked to tax code “V0” with a 0% tax rate was configured for the availability bonus. This was done to ensure that the availability bonus remains distinguishable from the discharging remuneration during invoicing and is displayed as a separate line on the print document: 
 Chart of Accounts 2500 – Account assignment for availability bonus 

 Tax code V0 – 0% tax rate 

 For the purpose of this blog, the availability bonus is modelled as a separate remuneration for the availability service rather than as a discount that is simply deducted from the energy charge. The actual tax and accounting treatment would depend on the applicable commercial and regulatory framework and is outside the scope of this blog. 
 Now we can finally execute the invoicing run and review the results: 
 Scenario 1 – Print document 2000000226 

 Scenario 2 – Print document 2000000227 

 As illustrated by the examples above, the availability bonus is displayed as a separate line on the print document, without any tax amount being calculated. 

 With the billing rate, quantity-based prices and corresponding rate determination configured, the two V2G scenarios can now be billed using the quantities registered by the devices. 
 The examples demonstrate that standard SAP IS-U billing functionality can be used to calculate amounts for both energy quantities measured in kWh and connection time originally recorded in minutes and converted to hours. The same billing logic can be applied to both device setups, regardless of whether the kWh and MIN quantities are registered by a single device or by separate devices. 
 Most importantly, both the billing documents and print documents confirm the flow from the original meter reading results through quantity processing and unit conversion to the final calculated amounts. This demonstrates how standard IS-U configuration can be used to model and bill selected commercial aspects of a Vehicle-to-Grid scenario without requiring custom billing and invoicing logic. 
 In the next chapter, we will explore an alternative solution. Rather than managing the entire V2G meter-to-cash flow in IS-U, we will investigate how Convergent Invoicing can be used to calculate the availability bonus and integrate it with IS-U without having to maintain the MR results recorded in MIN.

title: SAP Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Private Edition, 2025 FPS02 – What’s New
author: gheorghe_ceres
text:
Hello everyone, I hope this article finds you all well. It is once again with great pride and excitement that we would like to announce we have delivered the latest updates for SAP Extended Warehouse Management for SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Private Edition, with the 2025 FPS02 release. With this release, we further enhance the Predictive Labor Demand Planning forecasting capabilities by introducing accuracy comparison, add extensibility features for the Advanced Shipping & Receiving integration, deliver business process optimizations and user experience improvements, in the Warehouse Order Streaming, strengthen our Suite Integration capabilities, including new Advanced Returns Management follow-on actions, and much more. 
 To find out more technical details and information on each feature (such as Customization steps) please review the link the corresponding “What’s New” viewer from the help portal in the title of the subchapters. 
 And we begin today’s article with a look at the new AI innovations. 
 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE 
 Our AI strategy for Logistics and Warehousing is driven by a clear ambition: to help businesses overcome the growing labor and resource challenges in warehouse execution. With this latest release, we continue to build on that vision, reinforcing our long-term strategy and moving another step closer to a smarter, more resilient warehouse operation of the future through intelligent predictive analytics that forecast current and future workloads and through new EWM Agents, which turns insights into executable actions. We enhance everyday warehouse activities with natural language-based interactions with Joule to streamline outbound processes. 
 Predictive Labor Demand Planning (pLDP) feature enrichment 
 Building up on the work we have done in the previous releases, with this latest update Predictive Labor Demand Planning (LDP) takes several steps forward, by introducing forecast accuracy evaluation, enhanced APIs support for packing and staging, and a range of user-experience enhancement across the KPI app, monitoring tools, and application logs. A standout addition is the new LDP forecast accuracy KPI card in the FIORI Warehouse KPI app, which uses a 7-day look-back to compare forecasted workload against actual results. Users can drill down by activity area or process step and toggle between absolute and relative deviation views, making it easier to adjust planning and spot trends at a glance. 

 On the integration side, the Handling Unit API and the Warehouse Order & Task API now support LDP workload recording for custom-built warehouse confirmation applications. Customers can now leverage the standard labor demand planning features, by enhancing their calling application and providing a start time for the corresponding activity, giving development teams greater flexibility into tailored workflows. 
 Furthermore, we deliver a new Odata service to support the integration between predictive Labor Demand Planning and the new Warehouse Workload Optimization agent, released in October 2026 for Early Adopter Care program and selected customer groups, as part of SAP’s Logistics Assistant. The agent will provide the relevant labor demand data to optimize workloads for various resources within the warehouse with accuracy and efficiency. 
 Please take a look at the collective SAP note 3577311 which collects the released features per feature pack and downport possibilities. 
 We will shortly release a separate blog post covering the release and functionalities of the new Warehouse Workload Optimization agent, so if you want to find out more about the new optimization capabilities available for SAP EWM, please stay tuned. 
 Joule: Talk to your warehouse in outbound processes 
 And that’s not everything we delivered in terms of AI functionalities with this release . Joule can now converse directly with warehouse users to streamline outbound processes through natural language. Whether you need to create, cancel, or confirm warehouse tasks, set or reverse the "Ready for Shipping" status, or post and cancel goods issues, Joule handles it all through a simple conversation, guiding users through multiple screens to get things done. Beyond executing actions, Joule also acts as a troubleshooting partner, helping users investigate blocking reasons on EWM Outbound Delivery Orders (ODOs) and guiding them toward quick resolutions. It’s a smarter, more intuitive way to keep your warehouse moving. 
 ADVANCED SHIPPING & RECEIVING 
 Integration between transportation and warehouse logistics is a significant contributor towards logistics efficiency, synchronizing process changes between warehouse and transportation, reducing overall logistics-costs by optimizing and streamlining freight planning with warehouse execution. To further tighten this integration, with this release we provide the following enhancements options. 
 Enhancement concept for product hierarchy integration – we have expanded advanced shipping and receiving with support for the Kit-to-Order (KTO) process, unlocking greater flexibility for outbound operations. This release enables KTO across multiple process variants, including warehouse-driven ODO split, transportation-driven ODO split, and late transportation-driven ODO split (triggered at loading completion), all designed with one clear goal in mind: keeping item hierarchies consistent throughout the end-to-end process. It’s worth noting that nested BOM hierarchies and inbound processes are currently out of scope. This enhancement options is fully supported for both embedded and decentral ASR deployments, giving you the flexibility to adopt it in the setup that best fits your landscape. 

 New SAP Global Trade Services (GTS) integration BAdI – we introduced a new Business Add-in (BAdI) for SAP Global Trade Services (GTS) integration, giving customers even greater flexibility when it comes to compliance checks in outbound processes. Through the existing BAdI /SCWM/EX_GTS_PARAMETERS, additional products, such as components of finished articles that aren’t part of the EWM Outbound Delivery Order, can now be included in the GTS compliance check. Complementing this, the newly introduced BAdI /SCWM/EX_GTS_CHECK_RESULT allows the compliance check results for those additional product items to be evaluated and the aggregated check result to be influenced. To keep the integration compliant, results can only be adjusted following a conservative strategy, meaning an "OK" result can be changed to "NOT OK", but not the other way around. As with our other enhancements, this feature is supported for both embedded and decentral ASR scenarios. 
 CONTINUOUS MODERNIZATION & SIMPLIFICATION 
 Our commitment to modernization and continuous improvements not only enhances functionality but also provides users with a seamless and intuitive interaction, helping businesses drive efficiency, optimize processes, and deliver superior experiences to their stakeholders. To that end, I would like to highlight the following features from this latest release. 
 Warehouse order streaming – pick path optimization 
 One of the biggest and exciting highlights of this release is the introduction of warehouse order streaming, also called the ‘Pick-Path Optimization’ for SAP Extended Warehouse Management. This powerful new capability, which is directly embedded in EWM, is designed to make order picking faster and smarter, particularly in e-commerce and retail scenarios where pick-card based picking of small orders is common. With this feature, EWM Warehouse Orders can be flexibly created or re-bundled based on local EWM optimization algorithms that take both the optimal pick path and the resource (type) layout into account, helping pickers move through the warehouse more efficiently and reducing unnecessary travel time. 
 The pick-path optimization supports different key process steps, including System-Guided RF Picking and/or Wave Release, and can be activated and configured flexibly per queue, activity area, and warehouse order creation rule to match your operational needs. To help you find the best setup, the feature also supports simulation and algorithm comparison, with results visualized directly through the EWM Graphic Warehouse Layout (GWL), making it easy to evaluate different strategies before rolling them out on the floor. 

 Renovation in Segmentation processes with EWM 
 We’re excited to introduce several comprehensive enhancements in EWM Segmentation, making it easier than ever to work with segmented stock across your warehouse processes. Previously, using segmentation required a dedicated characteristic in the batch master but with this release, that requirement is gone. For batch-managed products and articles, there’s no longer a need to enhance batch characteristics just to use segmentation, simplifying setup and reducing maintenance overhead. The new capability also allows the validation of the stock segment to be skipped when it meets your business needs. 
 To put this into context: while batch classification describes stock and its detailed properties (like expiration date, production date, or country of origin) without being limited to predefined values, stock segmentation offers a logical or commercial division of stock using predefined values, helping to improve planning, forecasting, and material distribution. 
 With this release, segmentation is supported across a broad range of processes, including inbound processing (with GR Preparation and RF Receiving), putaway with exception handling, outbound processing, ad-hoc warehouse tasks and movements, picking with exception handling, posting changes, staging for and receiving from production, MES-driven staging, physical inventory, Goods Receipt Preparation (GRPI) for production, stock migration via the Migration Cockpit, initial stock upload (via /SCWM/ISU), and the planned customer return process, giving consistent, end-to-end segmentation support wherever it matters. We have also created a collective SAP note 3734726 which contains all details including corrective notes, and customers can select to implement based on their business processes. 
 Other modernization and optimization enhancements 
 Aside from the highlights mentioned above, here is a quick rundown of some more optimization and modernization enhancements delivered with this release: 
 Close HU in RF Packing Transaction – we have enhanced the Radio Frequency (RF) Packing transaction. Now users can close Handling Unit packing steps (process-oriented storage control) directly from the RF packing transaction without having to navigate to a separate transaction. 
 ERP Integration for Migration Cockpit – we enabled stock updates in ERP to happen directly during migration. This enhancement is particularly interesting for customers who run both – ERP (e.g. greenfield) and EWM (e.g. migration) transformation projects in parallel. To make this possible, a new EWM setting has been introduced that activates ERP integration for stock migration, giving you full control over when and how it’s applied. Best of all, the feature is supported for both migration approaches — staging tables and direct transfer — ensuring a smoother, more consistent migration experience regardless of the path you choose. 
 International Organization for Standardization (ISO) unit of measure support for WCU IDocs – with this feature, you can use units of measure supported by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in Warehouse Control Unit (WCU) IDoc communication. Using ISO-compliant units of measure contributes to standardized communication of quantities across SAP and external systems, reducing mapping efforts, and improving reliability of warehouse task processing across system boundaries. This feature adds new versions of the IDoc for sending and receiving WTs to a non-SAP system (IDoc /SCWM/WMTOID01) and the IDoc for confirming warehouse tasks (IDoc /SCWM/WMTCID01) that include fields

title: Quantum-Safe by Default: How SAP S/4HANA Closes the Door on Harvest Now, Decrypt Later Attacks
author: maya_s
text:
Quantum computers capable of breaking today's encryption may still be years away — but the attack on your data has likely already begun. Threat actors are harvesting encrypted network traffic right now, storing it for the day a quantum computer can unlock it. By then, it will be too late to act. 
 The good news: with CommonCryptoLib 8.6.2, post-quantum key exchange is now available for S/4HANA Public Cloud, Private Cloud, and On-Premise — and if your system meets the prerequisites, it activates automatically. No configuration required. 
 In this post, we explain why the quantum threat is urgent today, how SAP's hybrid post-quantum key exchange protects your data in transit, and what to watch out for when connecting to third-party systems.

title: Why SAP IBP Response & Supply Plays a Game No One Else Can
author: MarkusA
text:
Why SAP IBP Response & Supply Plays a Game No One Else Can 
 Order-based supply planning, native SAP S/4HANA execution, and the road to the autonomous supply chain 
 SAP IBP Response & Supply plans on individual orders and writes them straight back into SAP S/4HANA — a real-time, bidirectional link that reads and writes live execution objects, not a batch feed bolted on from outside. No external planning tool can match it. 
 The 2026 releases (2602 / 2605 / 2608) extend it: harmonized scenario management and AI-Assisted Scenario Planning with Joule , Characteristics-Based Planning with shelf life, Vendor Managed Inventory , Intelligent Deployment Conversion, and deeper native-execution integration. 
 The same foundation is what makes agentic, autonomous supply planning real rather than a demo: an agent that can act on real orders — governed and auditable — inside SAP's Design-to-Operate process. 
 Most supply chain planning tools answer the question "How much should we make next month?" SAP IBP Response & Supply answers a harder, more valuable one: "This specific customer order is going to slip by three days — here is exactly why, and here is what to do about it." 
 That difference is not cosmetic. It is the foundation of everything that makes Response & Supply hard to replicate — and the 2026 releases (SAP IBP 2602, 2605, and 2608) double down on it. This post puts the core differentiator in the center, then walks through the innovations that extend it. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Contents 
 1 The Foundation — Order-Based Planning and Native SAP S/4HANA Integration 
 2 The Gamechangers — What Cemented the Lead in 2026 
 3 Outlook — The Path to the Autonomous Supply Chain 

 The Foundation: Order-Based Planning and Native SAP S/4HANA Integration 

 The moat: order-based planning wired directly into execution 
 Many supply chain planning tools plan in time buckets and aggregated quantities . That approach has real strengths — and SAP IBP offers it natively: SAP IBP Time Series Supply Planning is purpose-built for organizations that want a less granular, aggregate view, where planning at the level of periods and total quantities is exactly the right altitude. But when a disruption hits, aggregate numbers can only tell you that a bucket is short. They cannot tell you which order is at risk, which customer is affected, or which single constraint is the culprit. 
 A real-time illustration: on October 8, 2026, three tankers were struck in the Strait of Hormuz. Petrochemical buyers and manufacturers worldwide knew within hours that a critical shipping lane had become a risk — but the decisive question remained unanswered: which specific supply order is on which vessel, and which production schedule depends on it arriving on time? Planners working from aggregate time-bucket views can only see that a bucket may go short. Planners working at order level can answer that question — and respond before the disruption reaches the production floor. 
 That's where the second engine comes in. Both run on the same unified data model — the same planning areas, master data, and key figures — so there are no batch handoffs or reconciliation between separate tools. Customers pick the right altitude for each part of their network, or combine both, entirely within one platform. SAP IBP Response & Supply plans on the level of individual orders — production orders, purchase orders, stock transfers, and customer sales orders. Two properties turn this into a genuine structural advantage : 
 1. Order-level granularity. Every planning result maps to a real order object. A planner can trace a delayed shipment down to the exact planned receipt and the exact material that is gating it. 
 2. Native SAP S/4HANA integration — no middleware. Response & Supply reads and writes real SAP execution objects directly through Real-Time Integration (RTI). Planned orders flow back into SAP S/4HANA and get executed, without ETL layers or nightly batch bridges. No external planning vendor can match this: they integrate to SAP through batch extracts and custom middleware, while SAP IBP does it via real-time integration and bidirectionally, as standard product. SAP IBP also ingests data from non-SAP ERPs and external sources through the integration framework and open APIs, so heterogeneous, multi-ERP landscapes are fully supported without giving up the deep execution link to SAP S/4HANA where it matters most. 
 Everything below extends this same principle: plan precisely, then hand the result straight to execution. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Two established differentiators built on that foundation 
 Order-level root-cause visibility. Because planning happens on real orders across the multi-level BOM, a planner can pinpoint the binding constraint behind a specific late order rather than staring at an aggregate shortage. That's the difference between an afternoon of investigation and a two-minute decision. 
 Transport Load Builder (TLB). This is a standout, long-standing differentiator. TLB consolidates deployment requisitions into optimized transportation loads that respect real capacity constraints — weight, volume, and vehicle/pallet limits — and rounds them to full-truck or full-container quantities so planners aren't dispatching half-empty trucks or overcommitting a lane. Crucially, TLB isn't a separate optimization silo: it sits directly on top of order-based deployment and native SAP S/4HANA execution, so the flow runs unbroken from supply decision → load plan → executed shipment. Standalone load-building tools exist; what they lack is that seamless line from order-level supply decision all the way to the loaded truck, in one system. 
 ________________________________________ 
 One cockpit for the planner 
 SAP has invested heavily in user experience. Response & Supply UIs are converging into Planner Workspaces as a single planning cockpit — a one-stop workspace to detect, decide, and act. Order review, projected stock, deployment, gating-factor analysis, and scenario planning increasingly live in one configurable workspace, so a planner moves from detecting a problem, to simulating a response, to releasing the orders — without hopping between disconnected apps. Fewer context switches, one consistent surface. → Demo: Planner Workspaces – In-Focus Alerts (1:28) 
 ________________________________________ 

 The Gamechangers: What Cemented the Lead in 2026 

 AI-Assisted Scenario Planning (SAP IBP 2608), on harmonized scenario management (SAP IBP 2602) 
 SAP IBP 2602 introduced harmonized scenario management — a single scenario model that unifies orders *and* key figures , with a full lifecycle (create, modify, promote) in Planner Workspaces, simulations layered on top of order scenarios, extended scenario lifetimes, promotion options that now include order promotion, and shine-through for orders — meaning unchanged active-version orders remain visible inside a simulation without being copied in. 
 (SAP IBP 2605 extended controlled shine-through for orders into the SAP IBP add-in for Microsoft Excel.) → Demo: Harmonized Scenario Management (3:23) → Release Blog: SAP IBP 2602 
 SAP IBP 2608 puts Joule on top of that foundation as AI-Assisted Scenario Planning . Through natural language, a planner responding to a supplier outage can ask Joule to assess the outage's impact all the way down to primary demand, delete orders for the impacted supplier, exclude that supplier from planning runs, and create new supply from alternative sources — turning a multi-hour manual investigation into a guided conversation. Because scenarios operate on real orders, the AI's comparison shows which specific customer orders each response protects or sacrifices, not just an aggregate service-level delta. → Demo: AI-Assisted Scenario Planning (5:09) → Release Blog: SAP IBP 2608 
 Characteristics-Based Planning for process, pharma, and food (SAP IBP 2602 & 2608) 
 Planning on SKU level isn't enough where two batches of the "same" product aren't interchangeable. SAP IBP 2602 combined Characteristics-Based Planning with Shelf Life Planning : define shelf life by characteristics , honor expiration dates of planning elements such as stock, and select the correct batch by evaluating both characteristics and remaining shelf life — directly targeting waste reduction and regulatory compliance in food and pharma. SAP IBP 2608 added SAP Best Practices content for CBP (on planning area SAPIBP2, with process/config/test assets) so that demands carrying characteristics are fulfilled only by matching supply. Very few planning platforms do this natively. 
 Vendor Managed Inventory (SAP IBP 2605) 
 SAP IBP 2605 introduced Vendor Managed Inventory with automated replenishment planning. Instead of the customer pulling replenishment, the supplier plans and triggers it: customer demand and inventory visibility feed the SAP IBP supply planning run, replenishment orders flow automatically to ERP via real-time integration, and exception-based alerts flag issues without disrupting the automated flow. A coordination handoff that normally lives in spreadsheets and EDI collapses into the same order-based engine. → Demo: Vendor-Managed Inventory (3:42) → Release Blog: SAP IBP 2605 
 VMI is also a foothold into a theme analysts and competitors weigh heavily — multi-tier supplier collaboration . Combined with SAP Business Network, order-based planning reaches beyond the four walls of the enterprise: forecast, purchase-order, and inventory signals can be shared with suppliers upstream, so the plan reflects what partners can actually commit to rather than an internal assumption. 
 Intelligent Deployment Conversion (SAP IBP 2602) 
 A new deployment conversion algorithm automatically converts stock transfer requisitions into deployment requisitions using only available-to-deploy supply (available stock, scheduled inbound). It converts by requirement-date priority — most urgent first — with configurable demand/supply horizons, backward-offset handling for past-due elements, inclusion of fixed Stock Transfer Requisitions, and splitting of Stock Transfer Requisitions on partial supply while respecting rounding values. It's the piece that turns a feasible supply plan into concrete, deployable orders — the natural feed into TLB and execution. → Demo: Deployment Conversion Run (4:34) 
 Deeper native-execution integration (SAP IBP 2608) 
 Three 2608 supply enhancements deepen the advantage by pulling more real SAP S/4HANA execution signals into order-based planning: 
 Quality Inspection Lots integrate in real time from ECC/SAP S/4HANA as a new SAP IBP order type, so stock tied up in inspection (with expected release dates and quantities) is respected in planning runs. 
 Procurement Scheduling Agreements bring scheduling agreement schedule lines into SAP IBP via RTI; SAP IBP pegs customer demand against confirmed schedule lines, reducing plan volatility. 
 Time-Dependent Yield lets yield rates vary by planning period during BOM explosion — relevant for semiconductors, pharma, food & beverage, chemicals, and discrete manufacturing. → Demo: Time-Dependent Output Coefficient (3:34) 
 ________________________________________ 
 Proof in practice

title: How Does SAP PLM Manage the Product Lifecycle from Design to Production?
author: reinitathomas
text:
A product goes through many stages before it reaches the customer—from the initial idea and design to engineering, testing, manufacturing, changes, and eventually end-of-life. 
 This raises an interesting question: 
 How does SAP Product Lifecycle Management (SAP PLM) help organizations manage and control the complete product lifecycle? 
 In an SAP environment, PLM is not limited to product design. It connects different processes and teams to ensure that product information, documents, engineering changes, product structures, and manufacturing data remain aligned throughout the lifecycle. 
 Key SAP PLM processes 
 1. Product Design and Development 
 The lifecycle begins with defining and developing the product. Engineering teams create and maintain product-related information and specifications. 
 2. Document Management 
 Technical drawings, specifications, design documents, certificates, and other product-related documents need to be controlled throughout the lifecycle. SAP Document Management helps maintain versions and ensure that the right documents are available to the right users. 
 3. Engineering Change Management 
 Products continuously evolve. Changes to designs, specifications, BOMs, or other product information need to be properly controlled and tracked. Engineering Change Management helps manage these changes while maintaining traceability. 
 4. Bill of Material (BOM) and Product Structure Management 
 The product structure needs to be maintained accurately as the product moves from engineering to manufacturing. This is particularly important when managing relationships between Engineering BOMs (EBOM) and Manufacturing BOMs (MBOM). 
 5. Integration with Manufacturing 
 One of the key benefits of PLM is its integration with manufacturing processes. Product structures and engineering information can be connected with production planning and manufacturing processes, helping ensure that the product being manufactured matches the approved design. 
 6. Product Validation and Quality 
 Before a product is released for production, it may need to go through testing, validation, inspections, and quality checks. Integration with SAP Quality Management can support these activities. 
 7. Product Release and Change Control 
 Once the product is validated, it can be released for production. Release processes help ensure that only approved product versions and related information are used. 
 8. Changes During Production 
 Even after production begins, engineering changes may be required due to customer requirements, quality issues, cost optimization, or regulatory requirements. Controlled change processes help manage these changes without losing traceability. 
 9. Product End-of-Life 
 PLM also supports the final stage of the lifecycle, including product discontinuation and managing the impact on materials, BOMs, documents, and related processes. 
 The complete lifecycle 
 A simplified view of the SAP PLM lifecycle could be: 
 Design → Product Definition → Document Management → Change Management → Product Validation → Release → Manufacturing → Continuous Improvement → End-of-Life 
 Discussion 
 From your SAP project experience: 

 How are you managing EBOM to MBOM transformation in your SAP landscape? 

 How do you manage Engineering Change Management and approvals? 

 How closely is SAP PLM integrated with SAP Manufacturing and SAP QM in your projects? 

 How do you maintain version control and traceability for product-related documents and changes? 

 What challenges have you faced when managing engineering changes after the product has already entered production ? 
 I would be very interested to hear how different organizations are implementing SAP PLM and how these processes work in real-world projects. 
 What does your SAP PLM lifecycle look like—from the first design idea to production and eventually product retirement?

title: SAP Showcases the Autonomous Enterprise in Action
author: Paul Taylor
text:
Just five months after promising customers that it would enable them to become AI-native autonomous enterprises , SAP has delivered: showcasing it with on-stage demos and live customers at SAP Connect in Las Vegas. 
 SAP Connect in 2026: Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 “It’s time to show you the Autonomous Enterprise in action underpinned by great customer stories,” SAP CEO Christian Klein told his keynote audience at the start of the event. 

 Klein reminded the audience that SAP introduced the Autonomous Enterprise at its SAP Sapphire conference in May 2026 as “the beginning of better.” Since then, he said, SAP has worked with hundreds of customers to implement Joule Work as the AI engagement layer for the Autonomous Enterprise. 

 A new UI for AI 

 “This month, we are rolling out Joule Work for all customers,” Klein said, describing it as a new UI for AI. He noted that for decades, users had to learn how SAP worked, but with Joule Work, SAP learns how people work. “From now on, the more than 400 million SAP users can talk in their own language to SAP, and Joule Work gets the job done.” 

 The Autonomous Enterprise in Action | SAP Connect 2026 

 Click the button below to load the content from YouTube. 

 Always allow YouTube 

 Video by Matt Dillman and Rana Hamzakadi 

 Klein explained that Joule Work is based on three pillars: conversations, where users ask questions and delegate tasks to agents; spaces, which display content, insights, and shared work; and Joule Studio, where customers extend Joule or build agents tailored to their own processes. 

 He called SAP’s deep business and data context its “secret sauce.” That context includes SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than 7 million data fields, 50 million tables, more than 50,000 public and private APIs, 400 data products, and extensive process knowledge. “That’s why Joule doesn’t guess,” he said. 

 SAP’s 110,000 employees are already using Joule to perform hundreds of thousands of tasks every day, he shared: “We are already seeing productivity gains in central functions like HR, finance, and procurement of over 20% and even bigger gains in more complex analytical and planning tasks.” 

 SAP Autonomous Suite 

 Klein then turned his attention to the SAP Autonomous Suite, the second layer in the Autonomous Enterprise. The suite initially covers five domains: finance, procurement, supply chain, human resources, and customer experience. SAP Autonomous Suite is designed for work where a good answer is insufficient and “the right answer” is required every time, he said. 

 “LLMs are probabilistic and only give you the most likely answer,” Klein said. He contrasted that probabilistic approach with SAP’s embedded agents. Because the agents operate within deterministic application workflows, they use the same data, follow the same rules, and leave the same audit trail as the applications themselves. Customers can choose the level of autonomy appropriate to each process, retaining human approval where risk is high and allowing greater automation for routine work. 

 Since SAP Sapphire, Klein said SAP has created more than 20 Joule Assistants and over 200 Joule Agents, and is aiming for more than 400 agents by year-end. “But the real story isn’t the number of agents. It’s the business outcomes they deliver,” he said. 

 SAP Business AI Platform 

 “These agents can only understand your business so well because of the SAP Business AI Platform,” Klein said. “The platform gives customers the best frontier model for every agentic use case, the deepest out-of-the-box business context and SAP-managed governance.” 

 Building on Klein’s remarks, Manoj Swaminathan, president and chief product officer of SAP Autonomous Suite, described the SAP Business AI Platform as the infrastructure that enables the Autonomous Enterprise. The platform is organized around three capabilities: building agents, contextualizing them with business data, and governing how they operate. 

 Swaminathan explained how the context layer makes agents more accurate. Joule Studio spans no-code and professional development and offers access to more than 70 models, a strategy he said reduces lock-in and controls token costs. 

 “Joule Studio is natively integrated with our context layer,” he said. “So, the agents you build are more accurate, faster to deploy, and more efficient to run. Our knowledge graph is the map with the processes, data flows, and business tools. The agents find the right processes among thousands and the right information among over 7 million feeds. SAP Business Data Cloud brings that understanding to all your data, one consistent view, the processes, policies, and logic to make it meaningful.” 

 Swaminathan said no AI can compensate for a broken data model. To help agents understand customers’ business rules, SAP Domain Models are trained on SAP’s code. For predictions, SAP provides two engines grounded in how a customer’s business operates: SAP-RPT, SAP’s model family trained on its business data, and the Prior Labs tabular AI mode 

 Jerseys from Jersey 

 During his section of the keynote, Jan Gilg, global president of Customer Success & Americas, used an imaginary startup – “Jerseys from Jersey” – to invite a handful of customers to the stage to answer his questions and validate aspects of SAP’s Autonomous Enterprise strategy. 

 The customers included Novartis, which is piloting Joule sourcing agents for bid analysis and negotiation support; Morgan Foods, which described a supply-chain transformation built on SAP S/4HANA and SAP Integrated Business Planning; Nestlé, which emphasized the importance of a unified digital core; and SAP customer and partner PwC, which spoke about the value of the Industry AI portfolio from SAP. 

 Summing up their comments, Gilg noted that the elements of the SAP Autonomous Suite “are more than a collection of functional components. It’s one system working together like connective tissue that provides connectivity, context, and control.” 

 Gilg also made several product announcements, including the launch of SAP Pay, an embedded payments service that can automatically execute and reconcile supplier payments once an invoice is approved. He also announced SAP’s planned acquisition of TechWolf , a Belgian workforce-intelligence startup designed to help close skills gaps. 

 Security and governance 

 In the closing section of the keynote, SAP Chief Security Officer Marielle Ehrmann focused on trust and governance. She noted that ransomware handovers that once took eight hours now take 22 seconds with AI, and while 83% of enterprises use AI daily, only 13% have real visibility into it. 

 “The biggest threat to companies is not malicious AI; it’s unmanaged AI,” Ehrmann said. To counter that threat, she said every agent should have a verified owner, a risk tier, and scoped access rights, supported by zero-trust checks on identity, purpose, and data sensitivity as well as human oversight. 

 She emphasized that SAP Business AI Platform incorporates regulatory and localization requirements, applies user authorizations, keeps customer data from being used to train foundation models, and supports three levels of oversight: human-in-the-loop approval, human-on-the-loop monitoring, and human-in-command override authority. “The more autonomously an agent operates, the tighter the oversight applied,” Ehrmann said, calling the principle “freedom within boundaries.” 

 A clear shift among customers 

 Wrapping up the keynote, Klein emphasized that trust is key to everything SAP does and has been for over 50 years. “We are delivering the most trusted and governed AI in the industry,” he said, but added, “AI also requires significant change management to ensure it delivers the desired outcomes for your business.” 

 That is where SAP’s business transformation solutions come in, he said. SAP Signavio measures process value before and after a change to help justify token spending; SAP LeanIX discovers and tracks AI agents; and SAP WalkMe supports user adoption and trust. Klein also highlighted an agent-led migration toolchain. Together, he said, these capabilities mean that the days of multi-million-dollar migration spend are gone 

 “This is no longer the start of something better. This is better,” Klein told the audience. He described a clear shift among SAP customers: “From manual steps to connected workflows, from reactive decision-making to predictive insights, from humans in spreadsheets to humans in and on the loop–all powered by our AI platform to keep AI accurate, governed, and extensible.” 

 And, most importantly, Klein said, “Its ready for you today… This is the Autonomous Enterprise.”

title: SAP Accelerates Autonomous HCM
author: Siva Sundaresan
text:
AI is reshaping jobs, skills, and ways of working at an unprecedented pace, pushing organizations to rethink not only their business models, but the workforce they need to support what’s next. 
 SAP Connect in 2026: Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 According to research from the SAP SuccessFactors Future of Work Research Lab , 72% of executives believe organizations claiming to transform work with AI are primarily automating existing processes rather than fundamentally redesigning how work gets done. Yet, 88% say redesigning work and roles creates significant enterprise value. And HR is ranked as the No. 1 owner of that work. As a result, HR and business leaders are looking at how technology can support their need to continuously align people, skills, and work with evolving business priorities. 

 This is the journey to Autonomous HCM . Autonomous HCM is the future of human capital management, where AI automates end-to-end processes, drives context-aware decisions, and optimizes workforce operations at scale. 

 As we think about Autonomous HCM, we have defined three pillars: 

 Automate the HR function to release capacity from administrative work: HR teams currently spend a significant share of their time on operational activities such as payroll, service delivery, recruiting administration, and workforce management. AI can reduce much of that burden, creating capacity for more strategic work. But automation is not the destination. It’s the foundation. The true value comes from what organizations do with the time and resources they regain. 

 Redesign how tasks, workflows, roles, and teams are structured throughout the enterprise, across both people and AI: For decades, companies optimized around jobs, functions, and fixed processes. AI challenges many of those assumptions. The opportunity is no longer simply to make existing work more efficient. It is to rethink work itself. This is not just a technology initiative. It is one of the most important business transformation challenges organizations face today. 

 Reinvent how organizations recruit, develop, move, and reward their people: Most talent processes were built for a world characterized by stable jobs and predictable career paths, but that world is rapidly changing. Organizations that succeed will create talent ecosystems that can adapt as quickly as the business itself. 

 These three pillars are all interconnected: automation releases capacity, work redesign determines how value is created, and talent-system reinvention makes the new model sustainable. 

 What makes this possible is SAP’s unique ability to bring together trusted workforce data, connected business processes, ontology, and AI within a single business context. Together, this context enables organizations to move beyond isolated HR activities and make strategic workforce decisions that drive the most urgent business outcomes. This context is what matters. 

 During SAP Connect, SAP announced that it has entered into an agreement for SAP to acquire TechWolf . TechWolf provides a leading AI work intelligence platform, which helps organizations understand the work their people do and the skills they have, giving them the right context and the right grounding. Once the transaction closes, TechWolf is expected to power workforce and talent strategies across the SAP SuccessFactors portfolio, bringing skills mapping, workforce planning, and organizational redesign informed by context from across the Autonomous Enterprise to guide decisions about development, deployment, and workforce transformation. 

 New Innovations to SAP SuccessFactors HCM Suite 

 While Autonomous HCM is our vision for the future, we have several new innovations spanning the entire SAP SuccessFactors HCM suite, available this month, including: 

 A growing portfolio of AI assistants 

 New AI assistants orchestrate work end-to-end and support decisions in real time. Many of the agents that we announced at SAP Sapphire are available this month, including assistants for payroll, HR service, learning, recruiting, onboarding, and career and development. We have more agents coming soon, including the new Workforce Planning Assistant to support customers using SAP Enterprise Planning . It is powered by connected workforce, contingent labor, and financial data from SAP SuccessFactors, SAP Fieldglass , and SAP Cloud ERP , to help business and HR leaders forecast workforce needs and create plans for the most effective mix of hiring, reskilling, redeployment, and external talent to address changing workforce demands. 

 Significant updates to our global benefits solutions 

 Benefits are among the most important decisions employees make, and they can also be some of the most complex for HR teams to support. To help make benefits administration more efficient for HR and benefits decisions more personalized for employees, SAP announced two new innovations built natively into SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central. The new agentic admin console for U.S. benefits provides HR administrators with a centralized view of benefits enrollment activity and exceptions, helping them quickly identify and resolve issues with built-in monitoring and natural language support. By reducing time investigating enrollment issues and navigating reports, organizations can improve oversight and manage complex enrollment periods more efficiently. Additionally, the new benefits decision support tool uses employee data already in the system to recommend coverage aligned to individual needs and budgets, resulting in a more personalized and intelligent enrollment experience for employees. 

 New integration of WalkMe Learning Arc with SAP SuccessFactors Learning 

 Creating and deploying learning content can often take weeks, making it difficult for organizations to respond quickly to changing business needs. With this new integration, learning teams can describe learning requirements in natural language, and AI generates courses and quizzes while maintaining author control. Learning experiences can then be created and deployed directly within SAP SuccessFactors Learning in hours rather than weeks. 

 Shaping Autonomous HCM with our customers 

 As we look forward , we know that what has worked in the past will not take us to the future. The goal is not simply to showcase technology, but to prove how connected AI can help organizations translate strategic decisions into measurable workforce and business results faster and more effectively. Rather than organizing our innovation around individual products or modules, we are focusing our innovation around the most important outcomes our customers are trying to achieve—and in doing so, leaning into SAP’s strength in connecting data, workflows, and processes across the entire SAP portfolio. We will co-innovate with select customers to define, validate, and measure outcome-driven approaches that connect workforce decisions directly to business value, proving the value of our innovations in real time. 

 The journey starts now 

 We are at a defining moment for HR leaders. The future of work will not be shaped solely by technology. It will be shaped by the leaders who can translate transformation into meaningful outcomes for their organizations and their people. 

 Autonomous HCM is the future of HCM. But it does not start tomorrow. The journey starts today. 

 To learn more about the latest SAP SuccessFactors innovations and how SAP is helping organizations advance their journey toward Autonomous HCM, watch the Success Connect keynote replay . 

 Siva Sundaresan is general manager and chief product officer for SAP SuccessFactors.

title: AI Can Act. Can Your Business Follow Through?
author: Balaji Balasubramanian
text:
At SAP Connect, we announced new and enhanced Joule Assistants for SAP Customer Experience, expanded SAP Order Management Services for complex B2B environments, and the general availability of SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition. 
 SAP Connect in 2026: Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 These announcements build on the Autonomous Customer Experience strategy we introduced at SAP Sapphire. That premise is straightforward: AI must understand customer intent, make context-aware decisions, and execute within business guardrails. Following through on a customer commitment requires AI grounded in real-time, enterprise-wide business data, with a deep understanding of the processes needed to orchestrate work from intent to outcome. 

 A quote needs accurate pricing and terms. An order depends on inventory, credit, payment, and fulfillment. A service interaction requires information about the customer, the product, and the commitments the company has already made. 

 Customers generally do not see this operational complexity. They experience whether the company followed through. 

 Joule Assistants move from providing answers to driving business outcomes 

 Many AI tools can reason about what should happen next and recommend actions. But executing complex enterprise processes requires more than that. 

 AI needs to understand the live state of the business, including customer commitments, products, pricing, agreements, orders, payments, policies, and operational constraints. It must then navigate the approvals, exceptions, and cross-application steps required to act. Without that grounding, proposed actions may appear reasonable but can be inappropriate, infeasible, or break down in execution. 

 This is the direction behind the latest Joule Assistant innovations. New and enhanced Joule Assistants for SAP Customer Experience combine role-specific intelligence with business and process context across marketing, commerce, sales, service, finance, operations, and compensation, helping users move from understanding what should happen to getting the work done. 

 The innovations apply this approach to moments where fragmented context, manual steps, and handoffs can slow the customer experience. 

 Campaign Assistant and Content Assistant help teams move from campaign ideas to execution faster by reducing the effort required to plan, create, refine, and activate marketing campaigns. 

 Shopping Assistant makes product discovery easier and more relevant to what the customer is trying to accomplish. 

 Quoting Assistant brings customer, pricing, and commercial context together so sellers can prepare quotes faster and spend less time assembling information across systems. 

 Service Planning and Operations Assistant translates service demand into coordinated plans, reducing the manual work required to align people, resources, and customer commitments. 

 Incentive Compensation Assistant and Recurring Receivables Assistant bring the same intelligence to critical processes behind the customer experience, helping resolve questions, reduce administrative work, and keep compensation and payment workflows moving. 

 The goal is not to add another conversational interface. It is to move work forward by bringing together the business context, process knowledge, and controls required to act. 

 Human judgment remains important where decisions require approval, oversight, or exception handling. Within defined guardrails, AI can assemble context, determine and execute appropriate actions, and escalate when human intervention is needed. 
 Campaign Assistant brings campaign performance, business context, and recommended actions together to help marketers move from insight to execution. 

 SAP Order Management Services coordinates execution across ERP landscapes 

 Order management becomes more difficult when an order crosses ERP systems, legal entities, plants, distribution centers, and business units. 

 Each transition can introduce different information about pricing, inventory, credit, fulfillment status, or ownership of the next action. Consolidating every ERP system before improving order execution is not always a practical starting point. 

 SAP is expanding SAP Order Management Services to provide highly scalable, resilient, real-time omnichannel order orchestration across SAP S/4HANA and other ERP systems. 

 Built on a cloud-native, event-driven architecture, SAP Order Management Services coordinates order execution across channels, systems, business units, and third-party partners without requiring organizations to consolidate their ERP landscapes first. 

 The expanded capabilities provide a common layer for validating orders, checking inventory across locations, coordinating transactions between business units, and monitoring progress through fulfillment. 

 This gives organizations greater flexibility to add, remove, and experiment across channels, while enabling the order management layer to detect disruptions, trigger exception workflows, and keep execution aligned with the original customer commitment. 

 In complex enterprise landscapes, this combination of scale, flexibility, and reliable integration helps businesses deliver consistent omnichannel experiences while improving operational efficiency. 
 SAP Order Management Services helps teams monitor orders, identify disruptions, and manage exceptions across complex fulfillment environments. 

 Complete business context across the customer journey 

 Customer intent enters the business long before an order reaches a fulfillment system. It begins when a customer discovers a product, engages with a campaign, requests a quote, or starts a purchase journey. 

 To deliver on that intent, customer-facing interactions must remain connected to the pricing, inventory, ordering, fulfillment, and financial systems that support them. 

 SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition , is now generally available. First introduced at SAP Sapphire, the edition allows midsize and growing companies to extend SAP Cloud ERP with commerce capabilities that use ERP data for pricing, availability, orders, invoices, and other transactional processes. 

 For more than a decade, SAP Commerce Cloud has supported some of the world’s largest and most complex digital commerce environments. With SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition, we are extending that approach to companies that want a more standardized, SAP-managed path to ERP-connected commerce. 

 By using SAP Cloud ERP as the system of record, organizations can connect digital commerce with pricing, ordering, fulfillment, and financial processes without building and maintaining those connections independently. The result is a faster path to value, lower operational complexity, and an ERP-aligned commerce model designed to scale as the business grows. 
 SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition, provides ERP-connected commerce with trusted pricing, availability, and ordering. 

 The same principle applies as customer interactions move across teams. A new native connection between SAP Engagement Cloud, enterprise edition, and SAP Sales Cloud synchronizes contact and company information while bringing relevant engagement signals directly into sales workflows. Instead of reconstructing customer context, sellers can continue conversations with a clearer understanding of prior engagement. 

 Customer experience depends on execution 

 AI can understand customer intent, make context-aware decisions, and act within defined guardrails. The harder question is whether the business can carry that action across the systems, teams, and processes responsible for delivery. 

 The innovations announced at SAP Connect address different parts of that challenge. Joule Assistants bring business and process context into the flow of work and help execute the next step. SAP Order Management Services orchestrates orders across complex ERP landscapes. SAP Commerce Cloud, cloud ERP edition, connects digital commerce directly with ERP pricing, availability, ordering, fulfillment, and financial processes. 

 Together, they advance a common principle: Autonomous Customer Experience depends on connecting customer-facing intelligence with the operational context and processes required to act. 

 Customers ultimately do not experience recommendations, models, or workflows. They experience whether the business followed through and delivered. 

 As AI begins to act on behalf of the business, the quality of that follow-through will depend on the business context, process knowledge, and operational reality behind every action.

title: Spoiler Alert: The Future of Work Is Already Here
author: Autumn Krauss
text:
Our Future of Work Research Lab at SAP SuccessFactors studies how jobs, organizations, leadership, and HR are changing and what those changes could mean for the future of work. 
 SAP Connect in 2026: Advancing the Autonomous Enterprise 

 Read the innovation news guide 

 Many of the futures we have explored are no longer hypothetical. They are showing up in how work is organized and experienced today. The fundamental question now is whether organizations are shaping those changes deliberately or simply reacting as they unfold. 

 Our latest research combines monitoring of more than 500 business, academic, government, and economic resources with original global mixed methods research involving 2,718 employees, 500 C-suite leaders, 60 HR executives, and founders of AI-native companies. It points to a fundamental concern: organizations may be optimizing the future of work for efficiency when they should be designing it for value. 

 The productivity trap 

 In October 2025, we explored 10 predictions for work, workforces, and work practices, each with two possible futures. A year later, the evidence is strongest for what we call the “AI Upgrade” future, in which AI’s value is measured through efficiency, productivity gains, and time savings. Signals of broader work transformation are emerging, but they remain less established. 

 The emphasis on productivity is understandable because time savings, output, and cost reductions are relatively easy to measure. The harder question is what organizations do with the capacity AI can create. They can ask employees to produce more of the same work, or they can redesign work, roles, teams, and talent systems around what people and AI can achieve together. 

 Work transformation needs a north star 

 Related research from our strategic work redesign program found that 88% of employees said their jobs have changed because of AI, yet half of those changes occurred without meaningful guidance from managers or their organizations. Employees are using AI to simultaneously offload tasks and expand the scope of their work, often without a shared playbook or a clear view of the intended outcome. 

 Before organizations can transform work intentionally, they need a clear north star for what work should become. Yet between 55% and 70% of employees said they had received no clear organizational guidance on the work shifts they are expected to navigate. At the same time, 72% of C-suite leaders said that most organizations claiming to transform work with AI are really automating existing jobs faster. Without a shared vision for work transformation, organizations risk defaulting to isolated experimentation and efficiency-first use cases, creating uneven outcomes and limiting the combined potential of people and AI. 

 Six shifts to guide better work design 

 We endorse six shifts in work and organizational design that are both enabled by AI and associated with work-enriching characteristics well established in organizational psychology as leading to increased employee motivation, effort, performance, and retention: 

 From specialist to generalist: Apply core expertise across a broader range of problems and tasks. 

 From static jobs to dynamic roles: Organize work around flexible responsibilities and outcomes that evolve with business needs. 

 From pyramid to diamond organizational design: Reduce coordination layers and concentrate more people closer to where core work happens, enabling them to own end-to-end delivery. 

 From output to impact: Evaluate work by the value it creates, not simply by activity or deliverables. 

 From centralized authority to decentralized decision-making: Move decisions closer to the people and teams with the context to act. 

 From people management to self-leadership: Give employees greater ownership of their direction, performance, and growth. 

 Through an experimental study, we validated how all six shifts can enrich work. For example, employees perceived 77% greater autonomy under decentralized decision-making, while dynamic roles were perceived as 49% more challenging than static jobs. The full report examines these effects across all six shifts, compares where organizations are today with where employees believe they need to be, and offers a prioritized path for leaders to get started. 

 Work transformation requires HR transformation 

 If work shifts this substantially, the function responsible for the people agenda cannot assume its own role and structure will remain the same. HR was built for fixed jobs, predictable career paths, established hierarchies, and talent systems designed for consistency. AI challenges each assumption. 

 With this context, we see HR’s new mandate as focused on three interconnected pillars: 

 Automate: Use automation and intelligent systems to release capacity from administrative work and create space for more strategic contribution. C-suite leaders estimate that 49% of HR work will be fully automated within five years, compared with 35% of enterprise work overall. 

 Redesign: Lead enterprise work redesign by determining how tasks, workflows, roles, and teams are structured across people and AI. Executives ranked work redesign as the transformation pillar that will create the greatest enterprise value over the next five years and identified HR as its leading owner. 

 Reinvent: Overhaul recruitment, development, mobility, performance, and rewards to support how work now gets done and who succeeds in the new way of working. Seventy-five percent of executives agree that organizations can succeed in the AI era only if they reinvent how they measure, reward, and grow people. 

 In the full report, we also explore four plausible futures for how these pillars might come together to shape HR’s strategic contribution, depending on where leaders believe the people agenda can create the greatest value. 

 The future of work is a choice
